content: 1. Patient care activities must be conducted in a clean and hygienic environment that supports practices aimed at preventing and controlling healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This includes ensuring the availability of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure, as well as appropriate infection prevention and control (IPC) materials and equipment. 2. A suitable environment, along with WASH services, materials, and equipment for IPC, is a fundamental component of effective IPC programs in healthcare facilities. 3. Senior facility managers and local authorities are responsible for maintaining an adequate hygienic environment. However, central governments and national IPC and WASH programs also play a critical role in developing standards and recommending their implementation to ensure proper WASH services, a hygienic environment, and the availability of IPC materials and equipment at the point of care. 4. The panel strongly recommends that materials and equipment necessary for proper hand hygiene be readily available at the point of care, despite the very low quality of evidence supporting this recommendation. 5. Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are among the most common adverse events in healthcare delivery, posing significant public health challenges due to their endemic burden and epidemic occurrences. They have a profound impact on morbidity, mortality, and quality of life, while also imposing a substantial economic burden on society. 6. A large proportion of HAIs are preventable, and there is growing evidence to raise awareness of the global harm caused by these infections, as well as strategies to reduce their spread. 7. Infection prevention and control (IPC) is a universally relevant component of all health systems, directly affecting the health and safety of both patients and healthcare providers. 8. Emerging global public health challenges, such as the aftermath of the 2013–2015 Ebola virus outbreak and the ongoing review of the International Health Regulations (IHR), highlight the need to support member states in developing and strengthening IPC capacity to build resilient health systems at both national and facility levels. 9. Strengthened IPC capacity contributes to achieving strategic goals, such as the WHO global strategy on integrated people-centered health services and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly those related to universal access to WASH, quality healthcare delivery, and reducing neonatal and maternal mortality. 10. The WHO guidelines on IPC core components aim to provide evidence-based and expert consensus recommendations for the essential elements of IPC programs required at national and facility levels to prevent HAIs and combat AMR through good IPC practices. 11. These guidelines are designed to offer a feasible, effective, and acceptable framework for developing or strengthening IPC programs, adaptable to local contexts based on available resources and public health needs. 12. The eight core components of IPC programs, as identified in the 2009 WHO report and subsequent reviews, form the foundation for these recommendations. The guidelines emphasize that all core components are equally important and essential for the effective functioning of IPC programs. 13. Countries and facilities implementing these core components may prioritize specific elements based on their context, previous achievements, and identified gaps, with the long-term goal of building a comprehensive IPC approach. 14. Effective IPC implementation is integral to health system strengthening and contributes significantly to reducing the burden of HAIs and AMR, including outbreaks of highly transmissible diseases. 15. Access to healthcare services designed to minimize the risk of avoidable HAIs for both patients and healthcare workers is a fundamental human right. 16. Effective and integrated IPC is a public health priority, contributing to strengthening core capacities and health service resilience within the context of the IHR. 17. The prevention and control of HAIs play a significant role in achieving the United Nations health-related SDGs. 18. Effective IPC is a key determinant of the quality of healthcare delivery, essential for achieving people-centered, integrated universal health coverage. 19. The WHO guidelines were developed following a rigorous process, including systematic reviews, evidence synthesis, and expert consultations, to ensure their relevance and applicability. 20. The guidelines were informed by a diverse group of experts, stakeholders, and external reviewers, ensuring a comprehensive and balanced approach to addressing IPC challenges globally.
